items.title: 20.1.1 Thermodynamic Stability of Benzene and Resonance

source_refs.note: Topic 20.1.1 with the first Figure 20.1 (PDF 60-61), redrawn. The book gives both '158.5 kJ/mol lower than expected' and '152 kJ/mol lower'; 360 - 208 = 152 is used. The definition of resonance is added for the learning outcome.

blocks.text: Like alkenes, benzene has double bonds in Kekule's structure, but it is much more stable than alkenes. The evidence comes from heats of hydrogenation: the heat given out when hydrogen is added over a catalyst, giving cyclohexane in each case. Cyclohexane is the common low-energy reference point.

items: So 1,3-cyclohexadiene (two C=C) would be expected to release 240 kJ/mol, and the hypothetical 1,3,5-cyclohexatriene (Kekule's structure, three C=C) 360 kJ/mol.
Benzene actually releases only 208 kJ/mol, 152 kJ/mol less than expected.

blocks.alt: Energy level diagram with energy upwards and cyclohexane as the bottom line. Levels above it: hypothetical cyclohexatriene 360 kJ/mol, 1,3-cyclohexadiene 240 kJ/mol, benzene 208 kJ/mol and cyclohexene 120 kJ/mol, each with its ring structure and an arrow down to cyclohexane.
blocks.caption: Figure 20.1: Energy level diagram of hydrogenation of cyclohexenes and benzene (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 20.1).
blocks.long_description: Each level is drawn at its value above cyclohexane: hypothetical cyclohexatriene 360, 1,3-cyclohexadiene 240, benzene 208 and cyclohexene 120 kJ/mol.

blocks.title: Resonance and resonance energy
blocks.text: Benzene's pi electrons are delocalised over all six carbons. Resonance (delocalisation) energy is the extra stability this gives compared with the hypothetical cyclohexatriene: the actual heat of hydrogenation of benzene is 152 kJ/mol lower than the expected value.
